Crown Rot.scientific_name: Phytophthora spp. (heart rot); Ceratocystis paradoxa (butt and black rot)
Crown Rot.description: Rot of the crown or the heart of the plant. In the field it is most often caused by Phytophthora water moulds, which thrive in wet, poorly drained soil. Ceratocystis paradoxa (also called Thielaviopsis) rots the cut base of crowns, slips and suckers and enters fruit through wounds. Fusarium heart rot has also been reported in the Philippines. DOST-PCAARRD found Phytophthora heart and fruit rot common in Queen pineapple farms in Leyte and Camarines Norte.
symptoms: The white base of the youngest heart leaves becomes soft and rotten.
Crown or heart leaves turn yellow or brown, starting at their base.
Soft, water-soaked tissue where the leaves join, turning dark brown to black.
Leaves pull out easily, often with a bad smell.
Planting material with a soft grey to black rot at the base breaks off easily at ground level.
look_alikes: Bacterial heart rot (Dickeya) also rots the heart, with water-soaked spots in the leaf centre and a strong fermented smell. It is worse in warm, wet weather. Fungicides do not cure it, so ask the MAO to confirm which rot it is.
Sunburn or chemical injury browns the crown, but the base of the leaves stays firm and does not smell.
Mealybug wilt reddens and curls the leaf tips while the heart stays firm.
remediation_steps: Remove affected plants and fruit right away, on a dry day if you can (moving wet, rotting plants spreads bacterial rots). Bury them away from the field and packing area; do not leave them in the rows.
Clean knives, bolos and crates in 1 part household bleach (such as Zonrox) to 9 parts water, then rinse.
Improve drainage in the affected part of the block so water does not pool.

For field heart rot (Phytophthora), ask your MAO about a fungicide with dimethomorph, metalaxyl-M or fosetyl-aluminium. Dimethomorph worked best in 2025 field trials in Thailand, and all three have legal residue limits on pineapple in the Philippines. In problem spots, growers abroad spray these as protection before symptoms appear. Use only FPA-registered products and follow the label rate and harvest interval.
When you spray, wear gloves, long sleeves and a mask, wait the pre-harvest interval on the label before harvesting, triple-rinse empty containers, and write down the product, rate and date.
For rot on crowns, slips and suckers you will plant, dip them in a registered fungicide such as one with propiconazole or triadimefon right after you remove them.
Researchers in the Philippines found the fungus Trichoderma works against heart rot fungi. Ask the MAO or ISU whether a Trichoderma product is available locally.
Check the surrounding plants again after one to two weeks.
preventive_measures: Use disease-free planting material, from fields without heart rot.
Take planting material in dry weather, without leaving fruit pieces attached.
Adding chicken manure to the soil can help suppress Phytophthora.
Dry crowns, slips and suckers in a single layer with the cut ends facing the sun before planting. Do not pile them wet.
Plant on raised beds or well-drained soil, and avoid planting during heavy rain.
Avoid wounding the crown and fruit during weeding and harvest.

Fruit Rot.scientific_name: Mainly Ceratocystis paradoxa (black rot); also Fusarium and other fungi and bacteria
Fruit Rot.description: Rotting of the fruit flesh. The most common cause is black rot (Ceratocystis paradoxa), which enters through bruises, growth cracks and harvest cuts and develops mostly during transport and storage. Warm, wet weather at harvest makes it worse. Bacteria (Dickeya) can also cause fruit collapse, which fungicides do not control.
symptoms: Soft, watery rot under a shell that may still look normal at first.
Shell becomes dark, brittle and leaks juice, often with a sour or fermented smell.
In late stages only a collapsed shell with black fibres is left.
look_alikes: Sunburn makes a pale, dry patch on one side. It is firm, not watery, but it can turn into rot later.
Overripe fruit is soft all over and sweet-smelling, without a spreading dark patch.
remediation_steps: Take rotting fruit out of the pile or crate right away so it does not spread to others.
Bury rejected fruit away from the packing area.
Clean knives, bolos and crates in 1 part household bleach (such as Zonrox) to 9 parts water, then rinse.

Sell or process the remaining fruit quickly, and keep it shaded, cool and well ventilated. If you have cold storage, keep partly ripe fruit at 10 to 13 °C and ripe fruit at 7 to 10 °C. Below 7 °C the fruit gets chilling injury (black heart).

If losses are high, ask the MAO about a post-harvest fungicide dip such as prochloraz or thiophanate-methyl. UPLB trials showed post-harvest dips control black rot in stored fruit, and both have legal residue limits on pineapple in the Philippines. Use only FPA-registered products and follow the label.
When you spray, wear gloves, long sleeves and a mask, wait the pre-harvest interval on the label before harvesting, triple-rinse empty containers, and write down the product, rate and date.
preventive_measures: Harvest early in the morning on dry days, not in the rain, and do not throw, drop or pile fruit roughly.
Do not put harvested fruit directly on the soil, and keep it in the shade while waiting for transport.
Do not overfill or underfill crates; both bruise the fruit. Leave space for air to move around the load.
Never use harvest crates to carry or store chemicals.
Do not pack sunburnt or cracked fruit with good fruit.
Clean and dry crates and packing tables between batches.
Control mealybugs and other insects that wound the shell.

Mealybug Wilt.description: A wilt caused by viruses that the pink pineapple mealybug (Dysmicoccus brevipes) carries from plant to plant. Ants, mainly the big-headed ant, protect the mealybugs and move them around, so controlling ants is the key step. DOST-PCAARRD lists it as a major problem of Queen pineapple in the Philippines. Plants can carry the virus without showing symptoms and still give lower yields.
symptoms: Leaves turn red, then pink, and their tips curl downward and die back, often in an upside-down V shape down the leaf.
The plant looks limp, starting at the leaf edges, because the roots collapse.
White, waxy mealybugs at the leaf bases and roots, with ants nearby. Both the pink and the grey pineapple mealybug spread the virus.
Some plants seem to recover with healthy new leaves while the old leaves stay damaged; they can still carry the virus.
look_alikes: Drought stress also makes leaves red and limp, but you will not find mealybugs and ants, and the plant recovers after rain.
Crown rot makes the heart soft and smelly; mealybug wilt does not.
remediation_steps: Check the leaf bases and roots of wilting plants and their neighbours for mealybugs and ant trails.

Control the ants first, with ant baits placed along the field borders and near nests. Ants protect and carry mealybugs and make the wilt worse. Without ants, natural enemies like ladybird beetles and parasitic wasps can control the mealybugs.
Remove and destroy badly wilted plants.

If mealybugs are still many, ask the MAO about an insecticide such as one with buprofezin, spirotetramat or pyriproxyfen. These have legal residue limits on pineapple in the Philippines; use only FPA-registered products and follow the label.
Biological options tested on Queen pineapple in the Philippines include predatory earwigs and the fungi Beauveria, Metarhizium and Lecanicillium. Ask the MAO or ISU if these are available locally.
When you spray, wear gloves, long sleeves and a mask, wait the pre-harvest interval on the label before harvesting, triple-rinse empty containers, and write down the product, rate and date.
Check the block again after two weeks to make sure mealybugs and ants have dropped. Even young crawlers carry the virus, so look closely.
preventive_measures: Use planting material from fields with little or no wilt.
If you can control water temperature, soak crowns in water at 50 °C for 30 minutes before planting; this has been shown to clean them.
Do not plant a new crop right next to an old or infected one.
Plough around the field to break up ant nests, and keep field borders weeded.
Remove old crop residue that shelters mealybugs between cycles.

Fruit Fasciation.scientific_name: Physiological or genetic disorder (not caused by a pathogen)
Fruit Fasciation.description: A deformed fruit that is flattened, twisted or fan-shaped, sometimes with many crowns. It is not contagious. It is linked to very vigorous plants that are slow to flower, high soil fertility, warm weather, and calcium or zinc deficiency, and the tendency can be passed on through planting material.
symptoms: Fruit is flattened, fan-shaped or twisted instead of cylindrical.
Fruitlets are fused or crowded along one side.
The crown is widened or split into many small crowns.
look_alikes: Multiple crown has two or more separate crowns on a normal-shaped fruit; fasciated fruit itself is deformed.
remediation_steps: Mark the affected plants so you can find them again.
Do not take crowns, slips or suckers from these plants for planting.
Sell the fruit for processing or local sale where shape matters less; it is safe to eat.
Count how many fruits in the block are affected and keep a record each cycle.
preventive_measures: Take planting material only from normal, healthy plants.
Use a balanced fertiliser programme, and do not overfeed. Make sure the plants get enough calcium and zinc.
Cull off-type plants so they do not build up in the field.
get_help: Talk to the Echague MAO or ISU if more than a few fruits per block are affected, so they can check your planting material and soil.

Multiple Crown.scientific_name: Physiological or genetic disorder (not caused by a pathogen)
Multiple Crown.description: A fruit with two or more crowns. It is not contagious. Causes include genetic off-types in the planting material, sunburn of the plant top between open-heart and red-bud stage, nutrient problems, and chemical injury between flower induction and flowering.
symptoms: Two or more crowns growing from the top of one fruit.
A crown that looks split, crowded or unusually large.
The rest of the fruit looks normal, though it may be flatter and broader.
look_alikes: Fruit fasciation also can have many crowns, but the fruit itself is flattened or twisted.
remediation_steps: Treat it as a quality problem, not a disease. The fruit is safe to eat or process.
Do not use these crowns or slips as planting material.
Sort affected fruit out of the fresh-market grade.
Record how often it appears in each block. Growers abroad report it happens now and then and rarely costs much yield.
preventive_measures: Take planting material only from normal plants, and cull off-types.
Use a balanced fertiliser programme with enough calcium.
Avoid spraying chemicals that can injure the plant from flower induction until flowering.
Close planting reduces sunburn on the plant tops during hot months.
get_help: Talk to the Echague MAO or ISU if a block has many multiple-crown fruits, so they can check your planting material.

No Disease.description: No disease symptoms were found on this fruit. No treatment is needed. Keep checking your plants about every two weeks, including the leaves and the base of the plant.
look_alikes: Early mealybug wilt shows on the leaves (reddening, curling tips) before the fruit looks wrong, so check the leaves and the base of the plant too.
Sunburn makes a pale or yellow patch on the side facing the sun. It is not a disease, but sunburnt fruit rots more easily.
checks: Look at the whole plant, not just the fruit: the heart leaves, the leaf bases, and the base of the stem.
Pull one or two lower leaves apart and look for white, waxy mealybugs and ants.
Press gently around the crown and the base of the fruit. It should feel firm, not soft or wet, and should not smell sour.
Check the plants next to this one. Problems often start in a patch, not on a single plant.
If something looks wrong even though the scan says healthy, trust what you see and scan that part again.
scan_tips: Scan in daylight or good light, without strong shadows or glare on the fruit.
Fill most of the frame with the fruit, including the crown, and hold the phone steady.
Wipe the camera lens if the picture looks blurry.
Scan from two or three sides. A problem on the back of the fruit will not show from the front.
If the app asks you to retake the photo, move closer or change the angle and try again.
Rescan the block every two weeks, and sooner after heavy rain or if plants start to look weak.
